:::{#thm-lotus}
#### Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)

**Discrete case.**
For any function $g$ of a *discrete* random variable $X$:

$$\E{g(X)} = \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x)$$

**Continuous case.**
For any function $g$ of a *continuous* random variable $X$ with density $\p(X=x)$:

$$\E{g(X)} = \int_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \p(X=x)\, dx$$

:::

::: proof

We prove the discrete case.
Let $Y = g(X)$.
For each $y \in \rangef{Y}$, the event $\{Y = y\}$ is the disjoint union
of the events $\{X = x\}$ over the values $x$ with $g(x) = y$,
and each $x \in \rangef{X}$ belongs to exactly one such group.

$$
\ba
\E{g(X)}
&= \E{Y} && \text{(substitution } Y = g(X) \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(Y=y) && \text{(definition of expectation for discrete r.v.)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} \P(X=x) && \text{(countable additivity over the disjoint events } \{X = x\} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} y \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(distribute } y \text{ into the inner sum)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(} y = g(x) \text{ for every term of the inner sum)}
\\&= \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(the groups partition } \rangef{X} \text{)}
\ea
$$

The last step regroups a possibly infinite sum,
which is valid because $\E{g(X)}$ is defined only when the sum converges absolutely.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

LOTUS says that to compute $\E{g(X)}$,
we do not need to first find the distribution of $g(X)$;
we can compute the expectation directly using the distribution of $X$.
The continuous case is the density-weighted analogue of this argument,
but a fully rigorous proof needs the general change-of-variables
theorem for integrals against a pushforward measure --- approximating
$g$ by simple functions and passing to the limit --- which is beyond
this page's scope
[@billingsley1995probability; @gut2013; @CaseBerg01; @wp:lotus].

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-lotus}
#### Expected value of $X^2$ for a Bernoulli variable

Let $X \sim \Ber(\pi)$.
By LOTUS (@thm-lotus, discrete case):

$$
\ba
\E{X^2}
&= \sum_{x \in \set{0,1}} x^2 \cd \P(X=x)
&& \text{(LOTUS, discrete case)} \\
&= 0^2 \cd \P(X=0) + 1^2 \cd \P(X=1)
&& \text{(expand sum over } x = 0 \text{ and } x = 1 \text{)} \\
&= 0^2 \cd (1-\pi) + 1^2 \cd \pi
&& \text{(substitute Bernoulli PMF values)} \\
&= 0 + \pi
&& \text{(simplify each term)} \\
&= \pi
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-lotus-continuous}
#### Expected value of $X^2$ for a Uniform(0,1) variable

Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ ([uniform distribution](random-variables.qmd#def-uniform)),
so $\p(X=x) = 1$ for $x \in [0,1]$.
By LOTUS (@thm-lotus, continuous case):

$$
\ba
\E{X^2}
&= \int_0^1 x^2 \cd \p(X=x)\,dx
&& \text{(LOTUS, continuous case)}
\\&= \int_0^1 x^2 \cd 1\,dx
&& \text{(}\p(X=x) = 1\text{ on } [0,1]\text{)}
\\&= \sb{\frac{x^3}{3}}_0^1
&& \text{(antiderivative of } x^2\text{)}
\\&= \frac{1}{3}.
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-linearity-expectation}
#### Linearity of expectation

For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with defined expectations,
and constants $a$, $b$, and $c$:

$$\E{aX + bY + c} = a\E{X} + b\E{Y} + c$$

:::

::: proof

We prove the discrete case, applying @thm-lotus to the pair $(X, Y)$,
which is a single discrete random object with values $(x, y)$,
and $g(x, y) = ax + by + c$:

$$
\ba
\E{aX + bY + c}
&= \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} (ax + by + c) \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(LOTUS for the pair } (X, Y) \text{)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} x \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(split the sum; constants factor out)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} x \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}}\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} y \cd \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}}\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
&& \text{(exchange the order of summation in the second term)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} \P(X=x, Y=y)
 + c \cd 1
&& \text{(factor } x \text{ and } y \text{ out of the inner sums; total probability is 1)}\\
&= a\sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \cd \P(X=x) + b\sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(Y=y) + c
&& \text{(marginalize: countable additivity)}\\
&= a\E{X} + b\E{Y} + c
&& \text{(definition of expectation)}
\ea
$$

Splitting and exchanging the sums is valid because the sums converge absolutely,
since $\abs{ax + by + c} \le \abs{a}\abs{x} + \abs{b}\abs{y} + \abs{c}$
and $\E{X}$ and $\E{Y}$ are defined.

Beyond the discrete case, this proof does not carry over by replacing sums with integrals.
That replacement would need a joint density for $(X, Y)$,
and some pairs have none:
if $X$ is continuous, the pair $(X, X)$ has no joint density.
In general, expectation is an integral against the probability measure,
and the theorem is the linearity of that (Lebesgue) integral
[@billingsley1995probability],
which is beyond these notes' scope.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-linearity-expectation}
#### Expected total of two dice

Let $X$ and $Y$ be the results of two six-sided die rolls.
Each has expectation $\sumto{x}{6} x \cd \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{21}{6} = 3.5$, so:

$$
\ba
\E{X + Y}
&= \E{X} + \E{Y}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation with } a = b = 1, c = 0 \text{)}\\
&= 3.5 + 3.5
&& \text{(substitute)}\\
&= 7
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

This calculation does not need the rolls to be independent.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-linearity-affine}
#### Expectation of a linear function of one random variable

For a random variable $X$ with a defined expectation,
and constants $a$ and $c$:

$$\E{aX + c} = a\E{X} + c$$

:::

::: proof

For discrete $X$, this identity is @thm-linearity-expectation with $b = 0$.
For continuous $X$ with density $\p(X=x)$,
apply @thm-lotus with $g(x) = ax + c$:

$$
\ba
\E{aX + c}
&= \int_{x \in \rangef{X}} (ax + c) \cd \p(X=x)\,dx
&& \text{(LOTUS, continuous case)} \\
&= a\int_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \cd \p(X=x)\,dx
 + c\int_{x \in \rangef{X}} \p(X=x)\,dx
&& \text{(linearity of the integral)} \\
&= a\E{X} + c\int_{x \in \rangef{X}} \p(X=x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of expectation)} \\
&= a\E{X} + c \cd 1
&& \text{(a density integrates to 1)} \\
&= a\E{X} + c
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

Splitting the integral is valid because both pieces converge absolutely:
the first because $\E{X}$ is defined,
and the second because its integrand is a non-negative density.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-linearity-affine}
#### Expectation of a rescaled uniform variable

Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$, so $\E{X} = \int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
By @cor-linearity-affine with $a = 2$ and $c = 1$:

$$
\ba
\E{2X + 1}
&= 2\E{X} + 1
&& \text{(expectation of a linear function)} \\
&= 2 \cd \tfrac{1}{2} + 1
&& \text{(substitute } \E{X} = \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)} \\
&= 2
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\ea
$$

:::
